#### Breaking

![Snake River](https://bloximages.chicago2.vip.townnews.com/idahostatejournal.com/content/tncms/assets/v3/editorial/2/79/2798c93f-7984-4284-a0fa-502057a55e0a/69c8a9a3ea613.image.png)

Idaho Fish and Game Southeast Region fisheries staff conduct a fish population survey on the Snake River below American Falls dam in November 2025.

AMERICAN FALLS — If you have ever wondered what is swimming beneath the surface of the Snake River below American Falls Dam, Idaho Fish and Game biologists have been investigating.

And what they found last fall is enough to get any angler’s attention.

The Idaho Department of Fish and Game’s Southeast Region conducted a second fish population survey on the Snake River below American Falls Dam this past week, running from the Oregon Trail Boat Launch to the Pipeline Boat Launch. The survey built on a similar effort completed last November and gave biologists a post-winter abundance estimate for comparison.

The results from that first survey painted a vivid picture of what lives in that stretch of river. Fisheries staff captured and released 312 rainbow trout, 17 mountain whitefish, 13 smallmouth bass, 11 brown trout and 8 cutthroat trout. Other species documented included Utah chub, Utah sucker and yellow perch. The largest trout captured was a 26.7-inch brown trout. The largest rainbow trout measured 22.2 inches, with the majority of rainbows running between 16 and 20 inches.

The numbers were notable. Fisheries staff estimate there were about 2,000 rainbow trout in that single mile-long stretch of the Snake River during the survey — a level of abundance typical for Idaho rivers where rainbows are found.

The survey went beyond simply counting fish. Biologists tagged trout to track angler catch rates and evaluate how fish survival varies by timing and location of stocking. Tag reports will also shed light on fish movements — including when fish pass through American Falls Dam into the Snake River or make their way to Walcott Reservoir — giving managers a fuller picture of how fish use the entire system.

That is where anglers play an important role. If you hook a tagged fish in the Snake River, Fish and Game wants to hear from you. Reporting your catch through Fish and Game’s Tag You’re It! program at [idfg.idaho.gov/fish/tag/add](http://idfg.idaho.gov/fish/tag/add) takes just a few minutes and directly contributes to the science that shapes how this fishery is managed — from stocking decisions to regulations.

For more information about the survey and other fisheries management work in the Southeast Region, contact Regional Fisheries Manager Patrick Kennedy at 208-236-1262 or [pat.kennedy@idfg.idaho.gov](mailto:pat.kennedy@idfg.idaho.gov).
